messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 53
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Social Worker
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 52

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Enclosed Spaces: Enclosed or confined spaces, Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant, Thought Suppression: I try to push them out of my mind
  Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
  Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Reginald, a 53-year-old social worker, sat in his office, fidgeting with papers on his desk. His mind kept drifting back to that night five years ago when he was sexually assaulted by a stranger in a parking garage. The memory still felt like an open wound, and whenever it surfaced, Reginald was hit with intense shame and terror. He couldn't shake the feeling of vulnerability that lingered long after the assault. Reginald's wife had been worried about him for months, noticing how he would become withdrawn and irritable at random moments. What she didn't know was that Reginald had started to ruminate on ways to get even with his assailant. He would spend hours replaying the event in his head, thinking of all the things he could have done differently. The fantasies of revenge gave him a temporary sense of control, but ultimately left him feeling empty and consumed by anger. To cope with the anxiety that gripped him, Reginald started to avoid enclosed or confined spaces. He would take the stairs instead of the elevator, even if it meant climbing 20 floors. His colleagues noticed the change, but Reginald brushed it off as a desire for exercise. The truth was, he couldn't bear the feeling of being trapped. Reginald's work began to suffer as well. As a social worker, he often had to visit clients in unfamiliar neighborhoods. But since the assault, he found himself avoiding these visits or making excuses to stay in the office. His fear of not being able to assess potential dangers in new places had become overwhelming. Even simple tasks like grocery shopping became daunting challenges. Reginald's hypervigilance also started to affect his daily routine. He would frequently check behind him, expecting to see someone lurking in the shadows. When he was running late for a meeting or an appointment took longer than expected, Reginald's mind would start racing with worst-case scenarios. His brain had become wired to assume that delays were a sign of something bad happening. When memories of the assault surfaced, Reginald tried to push them out of his mind. He didn't want to relive the terror and shame, but it was hard to shake off. There were moments when he felt like he couldn't find words to describe what had happened. It was as if his brain had become stuck on that night, unable to process the trauma. Reginald's wife finally convinced him to seek help after she found him breaking down in tears one evening. He realized that he needed support to work through his emotions and develop healthier coping mechanisms. As Reginald sat in his therapist's office for the first time, he felt a glimmer of hope that he might be able to break free from the shackles of his trauma. What brought him to this point was the realization that his symptoms were affecting not just his personal life but also his work as a social worker. He couldn't bear the thought of continuing to live in fear, constantly looking over his shoulder or avoiding places and people. Reginald was scared of confronting the memories he had been trying to suppress for so long, but he knew it was necessary if he wanted to heal.
